title: Indian Students Protest at Alberta College After Canada Denies Post-Graduation Work Permits
excerpt: Portage College issues statement saying it is in contact with immigration authorities, as affected graduates are urged to seek legal counsel amid a broader surge in PGWP refusals.
body:
Indian students at Portage College in Calgary staged protests this week after their applications for post-graduation work permits were rejected by Canadian immigration authorities, raising fresh alarm about the obstacles facing international graduates in the country.

The college responded with a public statement acknowledging the situation, saying it is in discussions with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada over the rejections. Portage College urged affected graduates to seek guidance from qualified professionals. "Students seeking advice should consult either an authorized immigration lawyer or a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant," the college said, according to the Times of India.

What Went Wrong With the Work Permits

The post-graduation work permit, or PGWP, is the primary pathway for international students to remain and work in Canada after completing their studies. It allows eligible graduates to work for up to three years and is widely seen as the most direct route toward permanent residency through programs like Express Entry and Provincial Nominee Programs.

However, PGWP eligibility rules have tightened significantly since late 2024. Graduates of college diploma programs must now demonstrate that their field of study falls within approved Classification of Instructional Programs (CIP) codes, limited to five high-demand sectors: agriculture, healthcare, STEM, skilled trades, and transport. Graduates whose programs fall outside these categories — including many business and general arts diplomas — are no longer eligible.

Additionally, IRCC introduced mandatory language-test requirements effective November 1, 2024. College graduates must demonstrate English or French proficiency at Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 5, while university graduates require CLB 7. Immigration lawyers have reported a sharp increase in refusals tied to these requirements, with some cases stemming from a known technical flaw in IRCC's own application system that fails to provide a clear upload slot for language scores.

"It's not enough just to say, 'Here are some bank statements.' They may have to go the extra mile and say, 'Here's where the money came from.'"

— Michael Pietrocarlo, Border Pass, a Canadian visa assistance firm

A System Under Strain

The protest at Portage College is not an isolated incident. Over the past two years, international students across Canada — overwhelmingly from India — have staged demonstrations in provinces including Ontario, Manitoba, British Columbia, and Prince Edward Island, where some students maintained protest encampments for months.

Canada's study-permit rejection rate for Indian applicants surged to 74 percent in August 2025, according to IRCC data reported by Reuters. By 2026, some estimates placed the figure as high as 81 percent. The crackdown followed the discovery in 2023 of nearly 1,550 study-permit applications linked to fraudulent letters of acceptance, most originating from India. IRCC's enhanced verification system subsequently flagged over 14,000 potentially fraudulent documents globally.

The Indian Embassy in Ottawa has said the rising rejection rate "had come to its attention" but stressed that issuing study permits is Canada's prerogative. "We would like to emphasize that some of the best quality students available in the world are from India, and Canadian institutions have in the past greatly benefited from the talent and academic excellence of these students," the embassy said in a statement.

Limited Options for Rejected Graduates

For students whose PGWP applications are refused, the options are narrow and time-sensitive. Immigration lawyers say graduates can request reconsideration through IRCC's webform, submit a new application if they are still within the 180-day eligibility window from program completion, or file a Notice of Application for Leave and Judicial Review in the Federal Court of Canada — which must be initiated within 15 days of refusal for in-Canada applicants.

Students who lose status have just 90 days to apply for restoration. Without a valid PGWP, graduates cannot legally work in Canada and lose access to the Express Entry pathway that many planned their careers around.

The Canadian Immigration Lawyers Association has flagged the systemic nature of some refusals, noting that IRCC's IT system does not always provide a clear upload slot for language scores, creating situations where applicants who followed the system's own generated checklist are refused for missing documentation.

What It Means for Indian Students

The enrollment pipeline from India to Canada has already contracted sharply. The University of Waterloo, home to Canada's largest engineering school, reported a two-thirds decline in Indian student enrollment over three to four years. The universities of Regina and Saskatchewan have reported similar drops.

For the estimated 32,000 PGWP holders whose permits are expiring in the coming weeks, the choices are stark: leave Canada, switch to another temporary status, attempt the permanent-residency route, or remain without legal status. None are straightforward.

Jaspreet Singh, founder of the International Sikh Students Association and a former international student himself, recalled a time when government messaging encouraged newcomers to "Study, work, stay." That sentiment, he said, has faded. Some rejected applicants, he noted, "are happy they didn't come."

The Portage College protests add another chapter to a story that has reshaped the relationship between Canada's education system and its largest international student population. Whether IRCC will revisit its enforcement approach or provide relief for affected graduates remains to be seen.
image_caption: Indian international students in Canada face uncertainty after the country denied post-graduation work permits to students at a private Alberta college.
nri_angle: Indian students form the largest international student cohort in Canada, and PGWP denials directly threaten the study-to-work-to-PR pathway that thousands of Indian families have invested in.
